AlternateTargets: come back to life after the end
Senses.Note: Zen bends an ordinary death-and-revival image into a stock saying repeatedly quoted in teaching-seat discourse and biographies. It belongs with ‘let go at the cliff’ (懸崖撒手), ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), and ‘gain life within death’ (死中得活), but remains one figurative referent rather than separate literal and technical objects. Frozen-corpus concordance: 254 exact hits in 132 storage files representing 131 independent works.

Senses.Explanation: To revive after being cut off: the records use a death-and-revival image in a recurrent teaching-seat formula and in explicit criticism of that formula. Its dominant fixed formula is ‘let go at the cliff and personally assent and undertake it; revive after being cut off, and you cannot deceive anyone’ (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再甦，欺君不得). Records also place it after ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), beside ‘shed skin and exchange bones’ (去皮換骨), and compare it with a cold ember flaming and a withered tree flourishing again. The identified master explicitly departs from the inherited formula: ‘the former sages all wanted to revive after being cut off; I am not like that.’ The entry reports this recurrent sequence and its criticism without deciding what state the phrase denotes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何以諸方一槩提舉評唱，考覈古今，謂之通宗？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (湛然圓澄禪師語錄): an unnamed guest is the exact questioner in the appended dialogue; the question challenges appraisal-commentary as a supposed measure of lineage mastery.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: 客曰 introduces the guest’s question containing 評唱; the following 答曰 belongs to the respondent.

Senses.Explanation: Appraisal-commentary is the public written handling of old cases or verses, and the same word labels the resulting commentarial work or collection. Chan books make it a named layer of case literature: the named commentator addresses earlier verses, and the resulting appraisal-commentary can become a titled collection. Title constructions name Yuanwu Keqin appraising Xuedou Chongxian's verses, Wansong Xingxiu appraising Hongzhi Zhengjue's verses, and Linquan Conglun appraising verses associated with Touzi Yiqing and Danxia Zichun. Daguan Zhenke's signed preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wushan Jingduan gives the documentary sequence: 'from recorded encounters, verses on old cases were made; from verses on old cases, appraisal-commentary collections were made' (由機緣而頌古作，由頌古而評唱集). A poem heading by Guxue Zhenzhe speaks of 'burning Wansong's appraisal-commentary on public cases' (焚萬松評唱公案). Its verbal, nominal, and title constructions are grammatical deployments of the same activity and product, not separate dictionary senses. An appended dialogue asks why widespread raising and appraisal-commentary, used to examine old material, is called mastery of the lineage. This hostile question is a stance toward the same public commentarial work, not a second referent.
